Three things to read off a calibration plot, in this order.

**Where are the dots relative to the diagonal?** In the first half of the season the example reader's dots sit well below
it: his 70–75% calls came true 60% of the time, and his 90%-plus calls
85%. That's overconfidence, the commonest pattern there is: in study after study, people's
"90% sure" comes true well short of 90% of the time ([Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) cited the classic
review). The fix is mechanical. Pull the confidences in: when you feel 90%, write 80% for a few weeks, and watch whether
the dots climb toward the line.

**How wide are the bars?** A dot from 30 calls can sit ten points off the diagonal by chance alone; a dot from 300 can't.
The vertical bars are 95% intervals for that wobble.[^wilson] Where a bar crosses the diagonal, the gap may be noise. This
is why one game can't tell you whether you're calibrated: sixty calls spread over five groups is about a dozen per group,
and every bar would span more than thirty points. A season can. As a rule of thumb, wait for about 50 calls in a group
before you trust its dot: at 50 calls, a group that comes true 75% of the time has a bar about 12 points either side.
With five groups that's roughly 300 calls, five or six games of every snap.

**How spread out are the dots?** This is the one people forget. A reader who says 60% on every snap of a team that throws
60% of the time is *perfectly* calibrated: his single dot sits right on the diagonal. He's also useless; he never tells you
anything the team's pass rate didn't. What makes a reader good is
[**resolution**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-resolution): stating different confidences on
different snaps, and having those differences come true. On a calibration plot, resolution is the dots being spread from
the bottom-left to the top-right, with the 90% calls really coming true more often than the 60% calls. The Brier score
rewards both. Calibration is knowing how sure to be; resolution is knowing more.

**A Brier score you can read off the plot.** Each dot is enough to estimate what its group costs. If a group was stated
at $c$ and came true a share $h$ of the time, each call in it costs, on average,

$$
h\,(1-c)^2 + (1-h)\,c^2 .
$$

A group stated at 90% that came true 80% of the time costs 0.8 × 0.01 + 0.2 × 0.81 = 0.17 a call; the same calls stated
at 80% would have cost 0.8 × 0.04 + 0.2 × 0.64 = 0.16. Weight each group by its number of calls (the bars under the
plot) and you have the whole log's score, near enough.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the Brier score in three pieces"}
Allan Murphy showed in 1973 that the Brier score splits exactly into three parts:[^murphy]

$$
\text{Brier} = \underbrace{\text{reliability}}_{\text{calibration error}} \;-\; \underbrace{\text{resolution}}_{\text{knowing more}} \;+\; \underbrace{\text{uncertainty}}_{\text{the game's own}}
$$

Write each call as a chance of a pass (a "run, 70%" call is a 30% chance of a pass) and group the calls by that chance.
*Reliability* is the average squared gap between each group's stated chance and its actual pass rate: calibration error,
lower is better. *Resolution* is how far the groups' actual pass rates spread from the overall pass rate: higher is better,
and it's the only term that rewards reading. *Uncertainty* is $p(1-p)$ for the overall pass rate $p$: the part nobody can
remove, the same for every reader of the same snaps.

For the example log, games 1 to 8: reliability 0\.020, resolution 0\.075,
uncertainty 0\.244. Games 9 to 18: reliability 0\.009, resolution
0\.064, uncertainty 0\.238. The calibration error halved: that's the
reader getting honest, and it's the cheap kind of improvement, because it takes no new knowledge. Resolution slipped a
little, partly because the later games were a different mix of snaps, which is why the total Brier score moved less than
the calibration did. Raising resolution takes reading more, which is what the rest of this course was for.
:::

### Scoring the log in Python

Here's the scoring routine. It reads a log in the final form from [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) (you need
at least the `call`, `conf` and `result` columns, and `clue` and `game` if you have them) and prints everything this
section has discussed. It's run here on the example log, saved as `prediction_log_2025.csv`.



::: {#ed6f65c4 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def score_log(log, base_rate=None):
    """Hit rate, Brier score, skill against the base rate, and the calibration table of a prediction log."""
    hit = (log["call"] == log["result"]).astype(float)
    conf = log["conf"].astype(float)
    brier = ((conf - hit) ** 2).mean()
    p = (log["result"] == "P").mean() if base_rate is None else base_rate
    ref = p * (1 - p)                                   # Brier score of always saying the base rate
    print(f"{len(log)} calls: right {hit.mean():.1%}, average stated {conf.mean():.1%}")
    print(f"Brier {brier:.3f} (always 50%: 0.250; base rate: {ref:.3f}); "
          f"skill vs base rate {1 - brier / ref:+.2f}")
    groups = pd.cut(conf, [0.49, 0.575, 0.675, 0.775, 0.875, 1.0],
                    labels=["50-55%", "60-65%", "70-75%", "80-85%", "90%+"])
    table = (pd.DataFrame({"stated": conf, "right": hit})
             .groupby(groups, observed=True).agg(calls=("right", "size"), stated=("stated", "mean"),
                                                 right=("right", "mean")))
    table["gap"] = table.right - table.stated           # negative = overconfident
    print(table.round(3).to_string())
    return brier


log = pd.read_csv("prediction_log_2025.csv")
score_log(log)
print("\nBy the clue you wrote down:")
log["right"] = log.call == log.result
print(log.groupby("clue").right.agg(calls="size", right="mean").round(3).to_string())
print("\nBrier by quarter of the season:")
log["part"] = pd.cut(log.game, [0, 4, 8, 13, 18], labels=["games 1-4", "5-8", "9-13", "14-18"])
log["sq_gap"] = (log.conf - log.right) ** 2
print(log.groupby("part", observed=True).sq_gap.mean().round(3).to_string())
```

And the calibration plot itself, for the whole season, in a few more lines:

::: {#cell-fig-calibration-code .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def calibration_plot(log, ax=None):
    """Stated confidence against the share that came true, one dot per confidence group."""
    hit = (log["call"] == log["result"]).astype(float)
    groups = pd.cut(log["conf"], [0.49, 0.575, 0.675, 0.775, 0.875, 1.0])
    t = (pd.DataFrame({"stated": log["conf"], "right": hit})
         .groupby(groups, observed=True).agg(stated=("stated", "mean"), right=("right", "mean"),
                                              calls=("right", "size")))
    ax = ax or plt.gca()
    ax.plot([0.5, 1.0], [0.5, 1.0], ls="--", color="grey", lw=1)          # perfect calibration
    ax.scatter(t.stated, t.right, s=t.calls / 3, zorder=3)                 # bigger dot = more calls
    ax.set_xlabel("stated confidence")
    ax.set_ylabel("share that came true")
    return t


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 3.0))
calibration_plot(log, ax)
plt.show()
```

calibration plot, not the raw score, is what shows him improving.

The `gap` column is the calibration plot in numbers, and the clue table is the one
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) told you to watch: a clue you lean on
often that isn't beating the snaps where you only had the situation isn't earning its place. Careful how you read it,
though: the two rows aren't the same kind of snap. The `sit` snaps are the ones where the situation alone was lopsided,
so of course they come true more often. The fair test of a clue is against a forecaster who can't see it, on the same
snaps: on the `align` snaps the example reader was right 66% of the time, and xpass, which
can't see the formation, 52%. That clue is earning its place.

### Reading your report card

Once a month, or at the end of the season, run the score and match what you see to a fix:

| What the score shows | What it means | What to change |
|:-----------------------|:--------------|:-------------------------|
| Dots below the diagonal, worst at the top | Overconfident | Pull every confidence in by about ten points for a month; cap yourself at 85% |
| Dots above the diagonal | Underconfident: you know more than you admit | Push the confidences out where the formation agrees with the situation |
| Most calls between 50% and 65%, and the dots flat (each group comes true about as often as the next) | Hedging; low resolution | Use the formation step: [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd) showed it's the one big move after the situation |
| Most calls between 50% and 65%, but the dots climb steeply and sit above the line | Underconfident, with good resolution | You're reading well; say so. Push the confidences out where the dots sit highest |
| Brier worse than the base rate | Badly overconfident, or your clues are pointing the wrong way | Check the calibration plot first; if the dots are near the line, score by clue and drop or reverse the one that's below 50% |
| Good on run/pass, poor on the second layer | Normal: coverage is hard | Keep second-layer confidences at 55–70%; check them against your chart |
| One bad game | Probably nothing | Look at the whole season; a game is too few calls to judge |

: A score is only useful if it changes what you do on the next snap.

### Scoring the second layer against your chart

Your run-or-pass calls can be scored from the play-by-play alone. The second layer can't: "zone, 65%" needs to know what
coverage was played, "five or more rushers, 60%" needs the rush count, "the run goes left" needs the direction. That's
what the chart is for. Join the log to the chart on the snap (your log has the quarter and the clock from Sunday, and
so does the chart), and score each second-layer call exactly as you scored the first: its confidence against whether it
came true.

Here it is on Super Bowl LX, with a second-layer call on every New England dropback: will Seattle play two-high or
one-high after the snap? The calls come from a scouting card, Seattle's 2025 regular-season two-high rate on dropbacks
by down, which is the kind of call a fan could make from [Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)
before the game. The chart is the one from the tendencies section above.



::: {#a512f1da .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
# Your live log's second layer for the game: one call per dropback, from the scouting card
# Seattle's 2025 two-high rate on dropbacks, by down (3 = third or fourth)
card = {1: 0.63, 2: 0.48, 3: 0.44}
log2 = chart.loc[chart.play == "P", ["qtr", "clock", "down"]].copy()
p_two = log2.down.clip(upper=3).map(card)
log2["l2"] = np.where(p_two >= 0.5, "2-hi", "1-hi")
log2["l2conf"] = np.maximum(p_two, 1 - p_two)                 # confidence in the call, as for the first layer

# Join on the snap, keep the snaps the chart could label, and score
scored = log2.merge(chart[["qtr", "clock", "shell_played"]], on=["qtr", "clock"])
scored = scored[scored.shell_played != "?"]                    # a "?" in the chart can't be scored
hit2 = (scored.l2 == scored.shell_played).astype(float)
brier2 = ((scored.l2conf - hit2) ** 2).mean()
two = (scored.shell_played == "2-hi").mean()
print(f"{len(scored)} coverage calls: right {hit2.mean():.0%}, average stated {scored.l2conf.mean():.0%}")
print(f"Brier {brier2:.3f}; always 50%: 0.250; "
      f"knowing in advance that two-high would come {two:.0%} of the time: {two * (1 - two):.3f}")
```

That's better than saying 50% every time, but not by much, and the reason is in the baselines. Seattle played two-high on 73% of these
dropbacks, against the 52% its regular season suggested, so calls aimed at the season's
habit were aimed at the wrong number for this game: most of them said one-high on second and third down, and most of
those were wrong. One game can't tell you whether that's a flaw in the calls or a game plan built for one opponent (here,
almost certainly the game plan; the last number in the printout is a hindsight bar no one could have reached before
kickoff). Over a season you'd score second-layer calls exactly as you score the first layer, with their own calibration
plot. Expect it to be flatter, with the dots bunched between 50% and 70%: the second layer is harder, and a reader whose
coverage calls are calibrated at 60% is doing well.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: Brier score or log loss?"}
[Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd) scored xpass with *log loss*, the average of
$-\ln(\text{probability you gave to what happened})$. It's also proper, and it's what most machine-learning models are
trained on. The difference is in how it treats confident misses. A 95% call that misses costs 0.90 in Brier and 3.0 in
log loss; a 99% call that misses costs 0.98 in Brier and 4.6 in log loss; a 100% call that misses costs 1 in Brier and
infinity in log loss. For a model, that's a useful alarm. For a human log, where one careless 99% would swamp a season, the
Brier score's cap is kinder and easier to read, and it's what the best-known forecasting tournament for people, the one
behind *Superforecasting*, used.
:::

## Where to keep learning

This is the end of the course, not of the subject. Four directions are worth your time.

**The coaches themselves.** Coaches teach each other in clinics: talks at the American Football Coaches Association's
annual convention, regional clinic tours such as Glazier Clinics and the Coach of the Year Clinics (for years sponsored by Nike, so older
notes call them the Nike Coach of the Year Clinics),
and the notes and videos that circulate from them.[^clinics] A clinic talk is a coach explaining
one scheme to other coaches, with the drawings, the rules, and the problems it solves; it's the closest thing to the inside
of a meeting room a fan can get, and it's where the "why" behind most of this course came from. Read them with the
vocabulary you now have, and with the habit from [Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd):
every scheme has a weakness the coach giving the talk is managing. Coaches have written good books, too. Bill Walsh's
*Finding the Winning Edge* is the classic on running an organisation and a game plan; for the ideas behind modern schemes,
Chris B. Brown's *The Art of Smart Football* and Tim Layden's *Blood, Sweat and Chalk*.

**The film-breakdown community.** A generation of writers and video makers now does on the internet what this chapter
asks you to do: All-22 clips, frozen frames, arrows. Ted Nguyen's All-22 breakdowns, Cody Alexander's MatchQuarters on
defense, Brett Kollmann's film-room videos, and the quarterback-focused breakdowns of JT O'Sullivan's QB School are good
places to start, and Greg Cosell's decades of All-22 study at NFL Films are behind much of the public vocabulary. Watch
how they work: freeze, rewind, one group at a time. Disagree with them when your own film says otherwise.

**The analytics community.** Everything in Part 13 came from people who publish their data and code for free. The
nflverse project (and its Python package, nflreadpy) is the foundation; Open Source Football collects worked analyses
with code; Ben Baldwin's writing explains the models behind EPA and xpass; and FTN's charting, free to use with credit
under its CC-BY-SA licence, is the public coverage and alignment data this course leaned on.

**The Big Data Bowl.** Every year since 2019 the NFL has released a slice of its player-tracking data and asked the public
to do something new with it, and its best entries have changed how the league measures the game
([Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)). The 2026 edition
asked about player movement while the ball is in the air; as of early October 2026 the 2027 edition had not been announced,
and past editions have opened in the fall.[^bdb] If you've done the course, you can enter it: you can read a play, chart one
and model one, and the `gridiron` library you've been reading diagrams from takes Big Data Bowl tracking files directly.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: a weekly routine"}
A season-long loop that fits around a job:

- **Sunday:** the live log for one team, every snap, with a confidence (one half if that's all you can manage).
- **Monday or Tuesday:** the film for that game. Step 0 and pass 3 on every snap; the full protocol on the 20 to 30 snaps
  that decided it. Fill the chart.
- **Midweek:** score the log, update your one-page card for the team
  ([Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)) from your chart, and pick one thing to
  watch for next Sunday.
- **Once a month:** the calibration plot, and the report card above.
- **In the off-season:** one project with tracking data, the Big Data Bowl if it's running.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: chart a full game"}
One game, one team's offense against the other's defense, end to end:

- **Before kickoff**, build the skeleton with `chart_skeleton()` from last week's game to test your setup, and write your
  codebook rules (the strength rule, where the box ends) at the top of a blank sheet.
- **During the game**, keep the live log exactly as in [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd): every snap, the checklist,
  a call and a confidence before the snap, and a second-layer call when there's time. When the offense goes no-huddle
  and you can't get a call down before the snap, leave that row's call blank rather than fill it in afterwards: a call
  written after the snap isn't a prediction.
- **The day after**, build the real skeleton for this game, and with the coaches film run step 0 and pass 3 on every snap
  and the full four-pass protocol on third downs, red-zone snaps, sacks, turnovers and explosives. Fill every film column;
  use `?` without shame.
- **Then score it.** Run `score_log()` on the game's log for the first layer, and join the log to your chart to score the
  second layer. Write down the three snaps that cost you the most Brier score, and the "because" line for each.
- **Keep the files.** One game is a start. A season of them is a calibration plot, a chart of a team, and the best
  football education you can give yourself.
:::

These drills are the film room's version of the course's habit: predict first, then check. The first two are pre-snap
frames from the film, and the question is what the next pass of the protocol will show. The third is a scoring drill.

**What coverage will pass 3 show after the snap, how sure are you, and what will you watch first to find out?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Single-high after the snap, about 60–65%, most likely Cover 3 with the boundary safety rotating down; watch the
*field* safety's first step.** The shell is two-high, but it isn't a balanced two-high: one safety is four yards shallower
than the other and pinched toward the ball. That's the tell from the tells catalogue in
[Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd): when two safeties disagree, the shallower, narrower one is usually the rotator.
He's already close enough to drop into a short zone on the boundary side at the snap (a
[buzz rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-buzz-rotation) if he goes to the hook area, a
[sky rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sky-rotation) if he goes to the flat), and the field safety, already wide,
would then run to the deep middle. Look at the slot on the short side, too: nobody is aligned over H. The pinched
safety is the only defender who can get to that area quickly, another sign that he's the one coming down. The corners
fit: off, outside leverage, eyes inside is the alignment of a corner who will bail to a deep third and keep everything in
front of him and outside him ([The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)), and the seven-yard
cushion is the zone-ish part of that clue.

Why not 90%? Because disguise is the norm ([Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)):
the pinched safety could be a quarters safety cheating to take away a slot route, or bait for a quarterback who reads
exactly this tell. The field safety's width argues the other way: he's well outside the middle of the field, and to
become the single-high safety he has to cover a lot of ground at the snap. And Cover 1 is possible too, with the same
rotation: the pinched safety comes down as the [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber) in the short middle
and the corners turn and run with their receivers instead of bailing.

What to watch: the **field safety's first step**. If he drives toward the middle of the field, the middle is closing and
it's single-high. If he backpedals straight, it's still two-high, and the pinched safety was playing a quarter or a half
from a cheated spot. Then the corners: bail (Cover 3) or turn and trail (Cover 1). On the chart: `shell 2`, then `cov C3`,
`rot B` if you were right (`B*` if the safety held his spot until the snap and only then came down).
:::
:::

**What will pass 1 show at the snap, which way will the run go, and which defender will nobody block?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A gap run to the right, most likely power: the left guard pulls, the line blocks down, and two defenders go
unblocked: the backside end by design and the walked-down safety by arithmetic. Run about 75%; right, about 65%.** Start with run or pass: second-and-4 from 21 personnel under center is a run look,
though eight in the box is the defense inviting play-action, so not 90%.

The guard is the scheme tell from [Watching Live](15-01-watching-live.qmd)'s catalogue: a lineman about to pull sideways
sets up for it, with less weight forward and a little depth. A pulling left guard runs to the right, toward the tight end,
so this looks like **power** ([Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)). What pass 1 should
show, if that's right, against this front: the center blocks *back* on the tackle shaded toward the pulling guard's
side; the right guard and right tackle double-team the tackle outside the guard and one of them climbs to the backside
linebacker; the tight end blocks down on the end over him; the fullback runs at the Sam, the last man on the line, and
[kicks him out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kick-out); and the left guard pulls behind the line and turns up through
the hole the kick-out and the down blocks create, looking for the middle linebacker.

**Who's unblocked?** Count it. Power brings seven blockers to this front (the five linemen, the tight end and the
fullback). The left tackle spends his on the gap the guard left, so six of them block a defender, and eight
defenders are in the box: two are free.
One is the defensive end on the *left*, the backside, left alone on purpose: he's too far from the play to matter if
it's fast enough. That's the trade power makes: it spends the backside guard to get an extra blocker at the point of
attack, and it accepts one free defender chasing from behind. The other is the strong safety, walked down outside the
Sam. Nobody has him; he's the defense's extra man, and the back has to make him miss. That's why runs into eight-man
boxes are so often checked to play-action, or sent with a receiver cracking down on the safety. If the film shows the
backside end making the tackle, the "because" line is about speed (the play was too slow, or the back hesitated); if
the safety makes it two yards downfield, the call lost to the eight-man box.

And if the line instead steps *together*, all to one side, with no puller, the guard's stance was a false tell: it's zone,
and you note it in your clue column.
:::
:::

**Which reader has the better Brier score? What's each one's mistake, and what should each change?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Reader B scores better (0\.187 against 0\.195), though both are making
a fixable mistake in opposite directions.** Both were right on about 75% of
calls, so the whole difference is in the confidence column.

**Reader A is overconfident.** His dots sit below the diagonal all the way up, and his 90%-plus calls, the bulk of his
log, came true only 81% of the time. Each of those misses costs between 0.8 and 1 in Brier score.
With the back-of-envelope rule from the calibration section: that group, 66% of his calls,
was stated at 97% on average and came true 81% of the time, so it cost
about 0\.18 a call; stated at its true rate it would have cost
0\.16. B's big group, the 70% of his calls at 65% or less,
was stated at 58% and came true 68%: about
0\.23 a call. The comparison is closer than the pictures suggest, which is why the
answer has to come from the numbers rather than the look of the plot. The fix for A: pull everything in. His calls already sort snaps well (his dots climb from left to right, which is resolution);
his numbers are just too big.

**Reader B is underconfident.** His dots sit *above* the diagonal: his 70% calls came true far more often than 70%. He knows
more than he admits, and he never stated more than 85% on any snap. The fix: push the confidences
out where the clues agree, toward 90% on the empty-backfield, third-and-long snaps.

How much is at stake? If each reader replaced every stated confidence with the rate at which those calls actually came
true (perfect calibration, the same calls), A's Brier score would fall to 0\.173 and B's to
0\.172. Same reading, better numbers. That is the cheapest improvement in the whole course, and
the calibration plot is how you find it.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Film answers what Sunday can't.** The All-22 shows all 22 players for the whole play; the coaches film's end-zone angle
  shows the line. Use them to check your reads, not to rewrite them.
- **Four passes, in order.** Freeze at the snap and grade your read; then the line, the quarterback, the coverage, the skill
  players, from what sets the clock to what uses it; then one "because" line that says whose play it was.
- **A chart turns a game into rows.** Same fields, same codes, every snap, with `?` allowed. Let the play-by-play fill a
  third of it; the film columns are where your chart knows more than any public file.
- **Score with a proper rule.** The Brier score rewards being right and being honest about how sure you were; 0.25 is "I
  have nothing", and the base rate and xpass are the bars to beat.
- **Calibration is how sure; resolution is how much.** Read the calibration plot for which way to adjust, the spread of the
  dots for whether you're learning anything, and never judge either from one game.
